question: Explain the doctrine of the Incarnation of Jesus Christ, setting out the facts about it which the syllabus notes.
idealAnswer:
The word Incarnation comes from the Latin incarnare, which means "to make flesh", or in a general sense the bodily manifestation of a supernatural being. The idea that God or the gods have made themselves present among humankind in human form is widespread in the history of religions, but in Christianity the doctrine states that God, in one of the modes of his triune being and without in any way ceasing to be God, has revealed himself to mankind for their salvation by coming among them as a man. Livingstone K. Buama says that the word incarnation directs our attention to the bringing together in one person, Jesus Christ our Lord, of both Godhood and manhood, and that it has to do with how the eternal word became flesh. St. Augustine explains that the meaning of the Word being made flesh is not that the divine nature was changed into flesh, but that the divine nature assumed our flesh except without sin. The story of Jesus' birth is recorded only in the Gospels of Matthew and Luke; it emphasises the belief that God is with us, and it is historical.

The syllabus notes six facts about the Incarnation. First, Christ was Son of God from eternity: he did not come into being at his birth but has always existed as the Son of God, and it was through him that God created the universe. Second, it was by supernatural conception: though his birth was as normal as any human's, his conception occurred through the intervention of the Holy Spirit, so that he was born without the inherited human inclination to sin. Third, it upholds Christ's full deity, seen in his character, his claims and his conduct in performing miracles, forgiving sins and accepting worship. Fourth, it establishes Christ's full humanity: he was born into a Hebrew family, subject to the Hebrew law, and exposed to hunger, thirst, fatigue, sorrow and temptation, sharing the weaknesses of humankind except sin, and so qualified to be the unique go-between. Fifth, it explains Christ's unique personality: he is both God and man, in two distinct natures and one person for ever. Sixth, it validates Christ's saving ministry: truly God and truly man, he is the one Saviour humankind needs, and by laying aside his eternal splendour and dying on the cross he becomes the reconciler between God and humankind.
keyPoints: Incarnation comes from the Latin incarnare, 'to make flesh'
God, without ceasing to be God, came among humankind as a man for their salvation
Augustine: the divine nature assumed our flesh, it was not changed into flesh
The birth story is recorded only in Matthew and Luke
Christ was Son of God from eternity; the universe was created through him
Supernatural conception by the Holy Spirit, so that he was born without sin
It upholds Christ's full deity and establishes his full humanity
It explains his unique personality (two natures, one person) and validates his saving ministry

topic: The Necessity of the Virgin Birth
question: Discuss the reasons why the virgin birth was a necessity.
idealAnswer:
The Virgin Birth, or Parthenogenesis, is the biblical doctrine that Jesus was miraculously begotten by God and born of Mary, who was a virgin. The term explains the way in which the Son of God entered human existence: it means that Mary had not had sexual relations with any man when she conceived Jesus. The syllabus gives three reasons why this was a necessity.

The first is Christ's pre-existence. The Bible teaches that the Word who became flesh was with God from the very beginning, and the pre-existence of Christ is testified many times in the New Testament. When Jesus came into the world he was not a newly-created individual such as we are, but was rather the eternal Son of God. To be born into this world of the Virgin Mary required divine intervention, and this is exactly what the Gospels record.

The second reason is the transmission of original sin. Jesus needed to be virgin-born because of his sinless nature. According to Ambrose and Augustine, both Early Church Fathers, the transmission of original sin is bound up with the sexual nature of propagation and the carnal desires aroused by procreation. That Jesus was conceived without any sexual relations explains how he was free of original sin. A basic New Testament teaching is that from the day he was born until the day he died, Jesus was without sin. To be a perfect sacrifice he must himself be perfect, without sin; and since our race is contaminated with sin, a miraculous entrance into the world was required, hence the virgin birth.

The third reason is Jesus' inheritance of the throne of David. If Jesus had been fathered by Joseph he would not have been able to assume the throne of David. According to the prophecy of Jeremiah 22:28-30 there could be no king in Israel who was a descendant of King Jeconiah, and Matthew 1:12 relates that Joseph was from the line of Jeconiah. Had Joseph been his father, Jesus could not rightly have inherited the throne, since he would have been a relative of the cursed line. The syllabus concludes that there are possibly other ways God could have chosen to send his Son into the world, but the way he chose was through the virgin birth.

question: Give an account of the Christological titles (the names) of Christ.
idealAnswer:
The many different names of Jesus Christ reveal the distinctive characteristics of his person and the work he came to do. The name Jesus itself means "the one who saves".

Messiah is the title the Jews gave to the future King who would descend from David; in Greek Christos, whence Christ; both mean "the anointed one". Simon Peter made the first clear declaration that Jesus was the Christ, but Jesus rejected the popular idea of the Messiah as a political deliverer from Rome, seeing his messianic role as one of suffering and death for the salvation of humankind.

The Holy One of God, given by Peter, belonged to him as the Messiah, especially set apart for God. Son of God occurs most frequently in John's Gospel and usually emphasises Jesus' deity; he was acclaimed Son of God at his baptism and given the title by the angel Gabriel at the annunciation. Jesus expressed his special sense of the fatherhood of God in the word abba.

Son of Man, in Hebrew ben adam and in Aramaic bar nasha, was a periphrasis for "man". Jesus used this title of himself more than any other. Though it seems to speak of his humanity, it points to his deity, for it is drawn from the book of Daniel, where the Son of Man rules an everlasting kingdom. Jesus used it when speaking of his earthly ministry, his death and his coming glory, and is thought to have favoured it because it carried no nationalistic associations, implied identification with humans, and had overtones of divinity and undertones of humanity.

Word and Wisdom: Jesus is designated the Word, or Logos, through whom God created all things and who is the perfect expression of God to humankind; he is also portrayed as the personal wisdom of God. High Priest, given to Christ in Hebrews, is drawn from the Old Testament sacrificial system, Christ's unrepeatable death making him the perfect mediator. Lord translates the Greek kurios; to call Jesus Lord was the mark of a true Christian and invited opposition from the Jewish authorities for blasphemy and from the Romans for treason. Unlike the other, descriptive titles, "Lord" expresses rank or worth, and "Jesus is Lord" is the ultimate Christian creed. Finally, Jesus is called God, as in Thomas's confession and in the classic text John 1:1. The Bible thus presents Christ as altogether God and altogether man.

subject: DOC
question: Outline the main aspects of Christ's ministry which distinguish him from any religious leader who ever lived.
idealAnswer:
Christ was unlike any prophet or religious teacher that ever lived. By his authority and deeds, and by the power of his teaching and example, he challenged his hearers to believe in him as the unique Son of God. The syllabus sets out six aspects of his ministry.

First, authority that convinced. The authority with which Jesus taught astonished those who heard him. The prophets of old repeatedly declared "The Lord says...", but Jesus directed his hearers towards himself, saying "But I tell you...". The Jewish leaders of his day took their authority from the great teachers of the past, but Christ taught in his own name and authority.

Second, parables that provoked. His teaching was given in terms and images understood in daily life, and this is particularly true of his unforgettable parables, which both concealed and revealed truth.

Third, miracles that confirmed. Christ's authority was further demonstrated by his miracles: the wind and the waves obeyed his command and even the dead were brought back to life. Most of his miracles were acts of healing that formed part of his mission of love, and they pointed to his identity as the Son of God and to the coming of God's kingdom.

Fourth, compassion that attracted. His deep concern for people was born of his understanding that human beings are created in God's own image but are also fallen and live in a fallen world. He showed care for the individual in his encounters with the bereaved, the sick and the demon-possessed.

Fifth, training that prepared. Towards the beginning of the second year of his public ministry the twelve disciples were chosen to share in his work of teaching, preaching and healing. They learned from his example and from private instruction, and were sent out, with some seventy others, to do his work. They did not understand all that was taught them at the time, but their training was vitally important for the future development of the Church.

Sixth, controversy that challenged. From the outset the words and actions of Jesus had a controversial cutting edge that finally provoked a collision with the Jewish authorities: he mixed with sinners, challenged traditions, liberated the Sabbath, and claimed to be God. Yet it is remarkable that while he directed his hearers towards himself he never gave the impression of being conceited, arrogant or selfish.

subject: DOC
question: Explain the importance of the atoning death of Jesus Christ.
idealAnswer:
The syllabus sets aside the many theories of atonement and treats instead the importance of the death of Jesus Christ.

It initiated a new relationship. Man's sin has created a barrier of guilt between him and his creator, but Jesus accepted the responsibility for human sin and willingly took its penalty on the cross. A new relationship is now available for those who respond to the good news that their sins can be forgiven; hostility has been replaced by friendship.

It fulfilled Old Testament scripture. The Old Testament showed that God and man could not be reconciled unless a sacrifice was made, for only then could the guilt of sin be removed. The Old Testament animal sacrifices could not in themselves take away sin, nor be a final solution to the problem of sin; the New Testament sees them as illustrations of the perfect sacrifice Jesus was to make.

It destroyed Satan's kingdom. The power of Satan's kingdom was broken through the death and resurrection of Jesus Christ. The final destruction of the Devil is yet to be, but the Christian is confident of victory through the power of the cross.

It reversed sin's dominion. The idea of redeeming, or buying back, a person who is enslaved is very strong in the Bible. Christ is presented as the one who by his death redeems his people from the penalty of God's moral law, and because he has taken our guilt upon himself, sin no longer has the power to dominate the life of the Christian.

It provided a way of victory. With the power of the Devil limited and the guilt of sin removed, the cross has set the Christian free - not free from the fight for moral purity but free for the fight. The tenses of salvation are these: we have been saved from the penalty of sin by a crucified Saviour; we are being saved from the power of sin by a living Saviour; we shall be saved from the presence of sin by a coming Saviour.

It guaranteed an eternity with God. The cross is the guarantee that God has set his eternal love upon his people. Death is still an enemy, but a defeated one, and like the Devil it will face ultimate annihilation. The work of Christ has often been stated in relation to his threefold office as prophet, priest and king.

chapter: THE DOCTRINE OF THE HOLY SPIRIT
topic: The Deity of the Holy Spirit
question: Discuss the evidence which the syllabus gives for the deity of the Holy Spirit.
idealAnswer:
The syllabus asks directly whether the Holy Spirit is God, and answers with several lines of evidence. The Spirit was associated with the work of creation; he gives the Christian new life; he is the source of all knowledge, the guide and helper of the Church in all ages; and he makes salvation a real experience to individuals. The apostle Peter equated lying to the Holy Spirit with lying to God. The Holy Spirit is the third person of the Trinity, and he is presented in the Bible as a person fully worthy of worship.

First, the Spirit possesses divine attributes. He is holy - and the syllabus notes that in the title "Holy Spirit" the word holy is not a noun but an adjective describing his character. He is eternal, omnipotent, omniscient, omnipresent, and he is truth. Each of these attributes is supported from Scripture: eternity from Hebrews 9:14, omnipotence from Genesis 1:2 and Job 26:13, omniscience from 1 Corinthians 2:10-11 and John 14:26, omnipresence from Psalm 139:7-10, and truth from 1 John 5:6.

Secondly, the Holy Spirit does things that only God can do. He was associated with the work of creation; he makes salvation a real experience to individuals; he gives the Christian new life; he is the author of the new birth; he makes prophecy possible; and he convinces people of righteousness and of judgment to come.

Thirdly, there is the descent of the Holy Spirit. One of the clearest indications of the full divinity of the Holy Spirit is given by Jesus himself when he promised to send the Spirit to the disciples. The Spirit is included in the Christian formula of baptism and in the apostolic blessing, and Peter equated lying to him with lying to God. When Christ had left the world, the Spirit was given his most specific work, and the book of Acts, which is the account of the early Church, portrays the Spirit as directing and controlling the new Christian movement. Taken together this evidence establishes that the Holy Spirit is God, the third person of the Trinity.

topic: The Emblems of the Holy Spirit
question: Describe the emblems of the Holy Spirit and state what each teaches about his nature and mission.
idealAnswer:
The emblems of the Holy Spirit throw light upon both his nature and his mission. The syllabus treats six of them.

Wind indicates unseen power, and the main ideas conveyed are mystery, sovereignty and energy. This vivid description of the Spirit's activity is used in Ezekiel's vision of the dry bones being given new life, in Christ's words to Nicodemus, and in the sound of rushing wind at Pentecost.

Water indicates life and cleansing. The key reference to the Spirit's work as water comes from words Christ spoke about streams of life-giving water flowing from those who believe in him; he was clearly talking about the life-giving activity of the Holy Spirit.

Fire indicates five things: the presence of the Lord, the protection of the Lord, the approval of the Lord, the purifying from the Lord, and the judgment of the Lord. The prophet Malachi predicts the coming of God's messenger in terms of refining fire, and this picture is reiterated in the New Testament when John the Baptist said that Jesus would baptize with the Holy Spirit and with fire. It is possible that the tongues of flame at Pentecost were meant to show the Spirit's refining activity.

Oil indicates light, healing, and anointing for service. In the Old Testament, anointing with oil was a sign that God had chosen someone for a particular task, and in this way priests or kings were set apart for God's service. The Bible tells us that Jesus was anointed by the Spirit, and this is also true for his followers.

The Dove indicates purity, peace, and modesty. The Spirit, in the form of a dove, descended upon Jesus at his baptism. Without doubt Jesus possessed the Spirit already, but this event pictures the gentleness associated with the dove, a gentleness which would characterise Christ's work.

A Seal indicates ownership, finished transaction, identification, security, value, authority and genuineness.

The syllabus adds an important caution: these images are nothing more than pictures meant to help us appropriately describe the work of the Spirit.

chapter: THE DOCTRINE OF THE HOLY SPIRIT
topic: The Work of the Holy Spirit
question: What is meant by the fruit of the Spirit? Explain the significance of the word "fruit" and outline the nine elements of which it is composed.
idealAnswer:
In Galatians chapter 5 Paul states the principle of fruit bearing: the fruit is produced by yielding to the sweet influences that are about us. "The fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, longsuffering, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, gentleness, self-control; against such, there is no law." It is important to notice that the word is singular - is, not are - and it happens to be singular in the Greek. There are not nine fruits, but one fruit composed of nine elements; the Holy Spirit produces one kind of fruit, that is, Christ-likeness.

The word fruit is significant for three reasons. It means the result, product, outcome or effect produced by the Spirit in the believer's life. Unlike the gifts of the Spirit, which are plural and only some of which are given to a Christian, each believer is to have all nine virtues composing the fruit of the Spirit. And as fruit on a tree takes time to grow and mature, so the Spirit does not cultivate these virtues in the believer's life overnight.

Love is what God is and what we ought to be, a selfless, sacrificial and practical love modelled on Christ's own. Joy is contentment and satisfaction with God and with his dealings, totally independent of circumstances, and differing from happiness. Peace includes the peace of God and harmonious relations with others; it is tranquility of soul and does not mean the absence of trouble. Longsuffering means patience in affliction, annoyance and persecution - patient endurance under provocation with no thought of retaliation, its supreme example being Luke 23:34. Kindness is graciousness and kindly disposition, best explained in the Lord's attitude toward little children. Goodness is kindness shown to others: kind but firm, ready to do good; it is love in action, expecting no rewards. Faith here means fidelity or faithfulness, which makes one true to one's promise and faithful to one's task. Gentleness is taking the lowly place, as Jesus did when he washed his disciples' feet; it is not weakness but controlled strength. Self-control is rational restraint of the natural impulses, a sign of strength and growth in character.

The fruit of the Spirit is not produced by human effort but as Christians live in communion with the Lord. It is the evidence of salvation and the genuine work of the Holy Spirit.

subject: DOC
topic: Some Heresies (False Views about the Trinity)
question: Explain the heresies of Modalism and Tri-theism, and state what the doctrine of the Trinity affirms in place of them.
idealAnswer:
The Church slowly formulated the doctrine of the Trinity in opposition to false interpretations of the faith, specifically over the deity of Jesus Christ. Two ancient trinitarian heresies are set out in the syllabus.

Modalism teaches that the one God assumes different forms, or plays different roles. In the beginning God acted as Creator and Law-giver; later in history, when things went wrong, he revealed himself as the Redeemer; and later still he revealed himself as the Holy Spirit who is the Enlightener and Sanctifier. Against this the syllabus insists that God did not as a matter of urgency become threefold for the purpose of creation, redemption and sanctification. As William Barclay emphasizes, God is always, from eternity, through time, and when time shall end, Creator, Redeemer, Sustainer and Enlightener.

Tri-theism pictures and presents the three persons of the Godhead - Father, Son and Holy Spirit - as consisting of three separate but co-operating Gods. Its emphasis is upon the Three-ness of God, but it overlooks the Oneness, the indivisible unity of God.

The early Church rejected both false solutions and worked out its own statement. Its alternative was not really a solution to the problem of how God is one and yet three; all it really did was to affirm both God's oneness and his genuine presence and work in Christ and in the Spirit. The one God makes himself known to us and works in our world and our individual lives in three different ways, but in each of these ways we have to do with the one God himself - not with three gods, nor with a hierarchy of divine beings, nor with masks which hide who the one behind them really is. The Westminster Confession puts it thus: "In the unity of the Godhead there are three persons of one substance, power, and eternity"; and the Belgic Confession says, "God is one in essence, yet distinguished in three persons." One essence or one substance originally meant that Father, Son and Holy Spirit are the same in being. It is very important to note that there are not three persons or personalities in God: God is only one person, and "one God in three persons" means one God who has at the same time three distinct ways of existence, exercised not in temporal succession but simultaneously.

subject: DOC
topic: The Relevance of the Doctrine of the Trinity
question: Discuss the relevance of the doctrine of the Trinity for Christian life and relationships.
idealAnswer:
The doctrine of the Trinity is ultimately a practical doctrine with radical consequences for Christian experience and life. God lives as the mystery of love among persons; and since we are created in his image and likeness, the question of what forms of life best enable us to live as Christ lived becomes urgent.

In our relationship with God, the doctrine is a way of contemplating the mystery of God and of ourselves in relation to him. The truth about both God and ourselves is that we are meant to exist as persons in communion in a common household, living as persons from and for others, not persons in isolation, withdrawal or self-centeredness. Christians are baptized into the name of the Father, Son and Holy Spirit; to live in the name of another is to appropriate their personal history and relational identity, so that our identity is linked intimately with theirs.

In our relationship with others, the Godhead reveals that God is truly a living one, personal and not impersonal, who deals with us at one and the same time as loving Father, self-giving Saviour and sanctifying Spirit. This helps us to affirm our own personhood and that of others, a moral obligation. The Triune God is Love: according to St. Augustine, without the Trinity there can be no fellowship as love in God; and Dr. Livingstone K. Buama says that love is the distinguishing characteristic of a true Christian, so that the practical demand is to abide in God's love and propagate it in word and in deed. The Trinity also teaches that God is indivisibly one, with unity of purpose and action, so that as we worship the God of unity we must pursue unity in our relationships. The three persons live in mutual co-existence, solidarity, fellowship and harmony, with no power struggle or personality conflict within the Godhead; those who embrace this are obliged to promote fellowship, solidarity and harmonious communal existence, and so freedom, justice, peace and prosperity.

The doctrine is also relevant to prayer. St. Augustine acknowledged the presence of the Triune God in Christian prayer, each Person playing a distinct role: we pray to the Father, who gives us power to become children of God; prayers are addressed to Christ, through him and in his name; and the Holy Spirit animates the prayer and enables us to discover God as our Father.

subject: DOC
topic: History of the Formulation of the Nicene Creed
question: Give an account of the history of the formulation of the Nicene Creed.
idealAnswer:
The formulation of the creed began with questions about the person of Christ: was he God or man? By the beginning of the fourth century the answer was not clear. One who attempted an answer was Arius, a presbyter from Alexandria. He said the Son, Jesus Christ, was a creature and not God; for him only the Father is unbegotten and self-subsistent, while the Son is begotten, so that there must have been a time when he was not. His main reason was that there is only one God: if the Son is also God, we have two Gods.

This view was strongly opposed by Alexander, Bishop of Alexandria, who suspended Arius from office. But Arius stuck to his opinions and gained support, so that the dispute threatened the unity of the church and of the empire. Emperor Constantine therefore summoned the first great ecumenical council of bishops at Nicaea in 325. The council condemned Arianism and drafted a creed to which all bishops had to assent. This was not the creed we now call the Nicene Creed, but it stated the essentials of belief so as to exclude any Arian interpretation. Its most noteworthy feature was its assertion that Christ is "of one substance as the Father", or of the same being as the Father.

In 328 Athanasius became bishop of Alexandria; earlier, in his treatise De Incarnatione, usually dated 318, he had already contributed to Christology, a "Christology of the Word, which took a body of the virgin": Christ the Word became man that we might become God, for only God, the Uncreated and giver of life, can save us.

The views of Athanasius triumphed some years after his death, at an ecumenical council at Constantinople in 381. It was this council which agreed what we now call the Nicene Creed, more accurately the Niceno-Constantinopolitan creed. It enshrined homoousios, "of the same being" or "consubstantial", as the most accurate term for the relation of Christ to the Father. At Nicaea the divinity of the Holy Spirit had been discussed but denied; at Constantinople it was officially accepted and affirmed, the Spirit being confessed as "The Lord and giver of life, who proceeds from the Father". Later, in the West and under the influence of St. Augustine of Hippo, the words "and the Son" were added, the Latin Filioque; the Eastern Church preferred "from the Father through the Son".

Alexander, Bishop of Alexandria, opposed him and suspended him from office
Emperor Constantine summoned the first great ecumenical council at Nicaea in 325
The council condemned Arianism; the creed of 325 asserted Christ is 'of one substance as the Father'
Athanasius became bishop of Alexandria in 328; his De Incarnatione is usually dated 318
The council of Constantinople in 381 agreed what we now call the Nicene Creed (Niceno-Constantinopolitan)
It enshrined homoousios, 'of the same being' or 'consubstantial', and affirmed the divinity of the Holy Spirit
The Filioque was added later in the West under the influence of Augustine; the East preferred 'from the Father through the Son'

subject: DOC
topic: The Apostle's Creed and its Explanation
question: What are the marks of a true church? Explain also what is meant by the holiness and the catholicity of the church.
idealAnswer:
The church of the New Testament was richly diverse; but despite all the local differences certain common elements stood out, and these are described as the marks of a true church. It accepts the full teachings of the Christian faith as spelt out in the Bible, that is, faith in Jesus as Messiah and Lord. It maintains continuity with the experience of Christians in the past - their unity and oneness of purpose, their love and joy, their devotion and purity of life. It celebrates the sacraments commanded by our Lord, that is, Baptism and Holy Communion. Its members follow the standard of life set by Christ, which is different from that of other people. It follows the apostolic preaching and instruction. And its members live in constant expectation of the coming kingdom of God.

The holiness of the church must be rightly understood. The basic meaning of holy is "different" or "separate". Since the Church is the body of Christ, and Christ is pure and blameless and was set apart for a purpose, so is the Church. To confess that the church is holy does not mean that its members are morally superior to other people; the church is holy because its members are called by God to live unselfish, pure and consecrated lives. The syllabus gives three ways in which the church is holy. It is a community of people who know they are sinners and freely admit that they are not good or superior - as Charles C. Morrison says, the church is not a society of good people but a society of sinners. It is a community of people not satisfied with themselves or with the way things are around them, gathered to admit that they need forgiveness and want to change. And it is a community gathered in the name of Jesus Christ who is its Head; the body is holy only because the Head is the Holy One.

The word catholic is probably derived from the Greek adverbial phrase kath' holou, which means "on the whole". Hence the Catholic Church means the Universal Church: it consists of all people throughout the world - races, nationalities, cultures, ethnic groups, social status and gender - who believe in Jesus Christ as Saviour and Lord. Though the word is not used in the New Testament, its meaning is expressed in Galatians 3:28 and Ephesians 4:4-6.
keyPoints: The New Testament church was richly diverse, but common elements are the marks of a true church
It accepts the full teachings of the faith - faith in Jesus as Messiah and Lord
It maintains continuity with Christians of the past and follows the apostolic preaching and instruction
It celebrates Baptism and Holy Communion, and its members follow the standard of life set by Christ
Its members live in constant expectation of the coming kingdom of God
Holy means 'different' or 'separate'; the church is not morally superior but called to consecrated lives
Three ways the church is holy: a society of sinners (Morrison), a community dissatisfied with itself, a community gathered in the name of Christ its Head
Catholic derives from kath' holou, 'on the whole'; the Catholic Church is the Universal Church of all who believe

subject: DOC
chapter: THE DOCTRINE OF THE LAST THINGS (ESCHATOLOGY)
question: Explain why the return of Christ is described as a practical doctrine and not merely an escape route for wishful thoughts.
idealAnswer:
The return of Christ occupies a prominent place in the Old Testament, in that most Old Testament prophecies concerning the coming of Christ deal not with the first advent, in which he died as our sin-bearer, but with his Second Advent, in which he is to rule as king. In the New Testament one verse in twenty-five deals with the Lord's return; the subject is mentioned 318 times in the 260 chapters, and it appears in every New Testament book except Galatians and the very short books such as 2 and 3 John and Philemon. Paul called the return of Jesus Christ "our blessed hope", and Peter called it our "living hope".

The syllabus insists that this is a practical doctrine and not merely an escape route for wishful thoughts. The early Christians expressed their belief in Jesus' personal return, a return closely associated with a period of great wickedness on earth, with the resurrection and transformation of their own bodies, with an earthly rule of the glorified Jesus, and with a final judgment of individuals and nations.

First, the early Christians acknowledged that their lives should be lived differently because of the return of Jesus. If we are expecting the Lord's return, that conviction ought to be seen in how we deal with social, political, economic, cultural and all other issues of concern. If we are motivated by prejudice, injustice, hatred, corruption, sexual immorality, abuse in all its forms, tearing down other people or wasting our gifts, then the return of Jesus has not made its proper impression on our thinking.

Secondly, it comforts those who are suffering. It helped the early Christians: as they suffered persecution and imprisonment, entered the arena to face the lions, or faced their executioner, they looked for Christ's coming and thought that perhaps in an instant Jesus would appear and call them home. Believers today have also lost children, parents and friends, and belief in the return of Jesus comforts them; the people of Paul's day had lost friends through death, and he reminded them of this blessed hope, saying "Therefore comfort one another with these words". The return of Christ is thus a practical doctrine because it is an encouragement to godly living and, at times, even to go on living, so that it bears upon present history as well as upon history's end.
keyPoints: Most Old Testament prophecies of Christ's coming deal with his Second Advent, in which he rules as king

It is mentioned in every New Testament book except Galatians and the very short books
Paul called it 'our blessed hope'; Peter called it our 'living hope'
The early Church associated the return with great wickedness, resurrection and transformation of bodies, an earthly rule of the glorified Jesus, and a final judgment
It is an encouragement to godly living: our conviction should be seen in our social, political, economic and cultural dealings
It comforts those who are suffering, as it comforted the persecuted early Christians
It comforts the bereaved: 'Therefore comfort one another with these words'
